```{r}
#| include: false
# Chunks that call a model are not evaluated; chunks that only build modules are.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = FALSE
)
```

A single signature can return several outputs, so start with one `module()`
call when the task is small. Split it into a pipeline when distinct steps need
their own instructions, models, or reusable pieces—or when cramming extraction,
summarization, and formatting into one prompt hurts accuracy.

A pipeline runs modules in order and passes each step's outputs to the next
step. Because a pipeline is itself a module, `run()`, `run_dataset()`,
`evaluate()`, and `compile()` all work on it directly.

## How data moves between steps

Step 1 receives the inputs you pass to `run()`. Every later step receives only
the previous step's outputs, plus any static inputs you attach to that step.
Pipeline inputs are not forwarded past step 1.

The example on this page turns release notes into a headline for customers:

| Step | Module | Receives | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `list_changes` | `notes`, the pipeline input | `changes` |
| 2 | `write_summary` | `changes` from step 1, and `audience`, a static input | `summary` |
| 3 | `write_headline` | `text`, which is step 2's `summary` renamed | `headline` |

## Build the steps

Each step is an ordinary module that does one thing:

```{r steps}
#| eval: true
#| message: false
library(dsprrr)

list_changes <- module(signature(
  "notes -> changes: list[str]",
  instructions = "List each user-visible change as one short sentence."
))
write_summary <- module(signature(
  "changes, audience -> summary",
  instructions = "Summarize the changes in two sentences for the given audience."
))
write_headline <- module(signature(
  "text -> headline",
  instructions = "Write a headline of at most eight words for the text."
))
```

## Connect them with pipeline() and step()

`pipeline()` takes modules in order. Wrap a module in `step()` when it needs
wiring:

```{r pipeline}
#| eval: true
release <- pipeline(
  list_changes,
  step(write_summary, audience = "customers"),
  step(write_headline, map = c(summary = "text"))
)
release
```

`step()` takes three kinds of wiring:

| Argument | Effect | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Named values | Static inputs, the same on every run. They win over an upstream field with the same name. | `audience = "customers"` |
| `map` | Renames fields from the previous step. Names are that step's outputs, values are this step's inputs. | `map = c(summary = "text")` |
| `select` | Keeps only the listed fields of this step's outputs for the next step. | `select = "summary"` |

Run the pipeline like any module. The result holds the last step's outputs,
here a list with one element, `headline`:

```{r run}
llm <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = "gpt-6-luna")
notes <- paste(
  "v2.3: Rewrote CSV export, now twice as fast.",
  "Added a dark mode.",
  "Fixed a bug that logged users out after five minutes."
)
run(release, notes = notes, .llm = llm)
```

## Chain with %>>%

When each module's inputs are exactly the previous module's outputs, `%>>%`
builds the same kind of pipeline with less typing:

```{r pipe-operator}
brief <- list_changes %>>%
  module(signature("changes -> summary")) %>>%
  module(signature("summary -> headline"))
run(brief, notes = notes, .llm = llm)
```

`%>>%` accepts only modules, so use `pipeline()` when a step needs static
inputs, `map` or `select`.

## Drop fields with select

Every output of a step moves on to the next one, and a prediction module
without a template writes every input it receives into its prompt—and warns
about undeclared extra inputs. `chain_of_thought()` adds a `reasoning` output,
so without `select` the headline step below would receive `reasoning`, warn,
and include it in the prompt:

```{r select}
#| eval: true
careful <- pipeline(
  list_changes,
  step(chain_of_thought("changes -> summary"), select = "summary"),
  module(signature("summary -> headline"))
)
careful
```

## When a later step needs an original input

Suppose step 1 extracts facts from a document and step 2 answers a question
about those facts. As a pipeline, `run()` stops with "Missing inputs for
pipeline step 2", because `question` went only to step 1. If the value is the
same on every run, attach it as a static input with `step()`. Otherwise,
write the flow as a function with `module_fn()` (see
[Choose a module type](advanced-modules.html)), which passes the active chat to
a `.llm` argument:

```{r module-fn}
facts_from <- module(signature("document -> facts: list[str]"))
answer_from <- module(signature("facts: list[str], question -> answer"))

qa <- module_fn(
  "document, question -> answer",
  function(document, question, .llm) {
    facts <- run(facts_from, document = document, .llm = .llm)$facts
    run(answer_from, facts = facts, question = question, .llm = .llm)
  }
)
run(qa, document = notes, question = "Is there a dark mode now?", .llm = llm)
```

The trade-off is optimization: `compile()` cannot see inside a function, so
it refuses `module_fn()` programs. Compile `facts_from` and `answer_from` on
their own instead.

## Run and inspect a pipeline

`run_dataset()` runs the pipeline once per row and returns the input columns
plus a `result` list-column holding the final step's outputs:

```{r run-dataset}
releases <- tibble::tibble(
  notes = c(notes, "v2.4: Added single sign-on. Search is faster.")
)
results <- run_dataset(release, releases, .llm = llm)
results$result
#> [[1]]: list(headline = "Faster CSV exports and dark mode arrive")
#> [[2]]: list(headline = "Single sign-on and faster search in v2.4")
```

To inspect intermediate steps, read the pipeline's traces (`step_inputs` and
`step_outputs`) or ask for `.return_format = "structured"`, which totals usage
across steps (`n_steps`, `provider_calls`, `total_tokens`, `cost`) and stores
each step's prompt and metadata in `get_metadata(result)$step_metadata`:

```{r step-outputs}
result <- run(release, notes = notes, .llm = llm, .return_format = "structured")
get_metadata(result)$total_tokens
cat(get_metadata(result)$step_metadata[[2]]$prompt)

latest <- release$state$traces[[length(release$state$traces)]]
latest$step_inputs   # list of length 3, one entry per step
latest$step_outputs  # list of length 3: changes, summary, headline
```

## Compile the whole pipeline

`BootstrapFewShot()` compiles a pipeline jointly: it runs the whole pipeline
on each training row and scores the final output with your metric. When a run
passes, every step's inputs and outputs from that run become a demonstration
for that step, so only the final output needs a label. Pass
`max_labeled_demos = 0L` on small training sets so rows are bootstrapped end to
end rather than consumed as labeled demos on the final step:

```{r compile}
past_releases <- tibble::tibble(
  notes = c(
    "v2.1: Added two-factor login. Fixed slow search on large projects.",
    "v2.2: New PDF export. Removed the legacy API."
  ),
  headline = c(
    "Two-factor login and faster search",
    "PDF export arrives, legacy API retires"
  )
)

compiled <- compile(
  release,
  BootstrapFewShot(
    metric = metric_f1(field = "headline"),
    metric_threshold = 0.5,
    max_bootstrapped_demos = 2L,
    max_labeled_demos = 0L
  ),
  past_releases,
  .llm = llm
)
```

`compile()` returns a new pipeline and leaves `release` unchanged. A useful
training set has more than two rows; [Compile and
optimize](compilation-optimization.html) covers data, metrics, and the other
teleprompters.
